newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission to debate environmental liability options.
newsitem.headline: Commission to debate environmental liability options.

text.p: The Eurpean Commission is due to discuss on Wednesday options for an EU-wide regime for environmental liability rules intended to make polluters responsible for the clean-up of any mess they make.

The Commission will consider three possibilities for an EU legal system, ranging from a directive for a general liability system, Community accession to the Council of Europe's Lugano Convention or a narrower directive on liability for environmental damage alone.

Wednesday's talks, limited to an orientation debate, take place against a backdrop of mixed member state positions on the need for any Community instrument. EU-level action is broadly favoured in some form by the largest grouping of countries according to a draft of Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard's planned communication.

Five states -- Finland, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands -- are signatories to the Lugano Convention on environmental liability while Austria has drafted national laws braodly in line with the convention, the draft said.

Germany, Britain, Denmark and France "are known to oppose the approach" mapped out in the Convention, according to the paper, the first three because it conflicts with their national regimes and the latter because of questions about Community competence to accede to the Convention. Britain has raised similar questions, it added.

Bjerregaard's concerns include worries that member state liability regimes risk creating a patchwork of different systems across the Community, including many which provide inadequate nature protection as required by the Habitats and Birds Directives, 92/43/EEC and 79/409/EEC respectively.

"A key reason for proposing action at Community level is precisely the political momentum on new environmental liability rules currently in evidence within member states. Commission proposals would be a direct response by providing a focus around which member state regimes can converge and filling certain gaps in member state laws," the draft said.
In the absence of adequate liability laws, damage to the environment remains unremedied or, ultimately, a matter for a clean-up operation funded by taxpayers.

"Once potentially liable persons are aware that they will have to pay for the environmental damage they may cause, they are very likely to be dissuaded from actions that might cause damage," the paper said, adding that such awareness should also encourage preventive measures and reseach and development efforts.

Other points raised by the paper concern access to legal systems for environmental non-governmental organisations, often the only bodies actively seeking remedy for environmental damage where no private party has an interest in taking action.
The paper suggests that any Community instrument should be based on strict liability, for future damage only, leaving to member states the tricky question of historical damage.
The "liable party should be the operator in control of the damaging activity, the most direct interpretation of polluter", the paper added.

"While in some quarters, there has been some opposition, there seems to be a clear majority in favour of taking some action. It's quite clear that we are going to do something concrete but I don't know what that's going to be yet," one Commission official said after Monday's preparatory meeting for the Wednesday meeting.
